topic: Michael Posner (1980): Covert Spatial Attention 'Spotlight' Without Moving Your Eyes
visual_mode_reason: Posner's central fixation cross with valid vs invalid peripheral arrow cues demonstrates covert attention cleanly in millisecond reaction time, directly governed by the dorsal frontoparietal orienting network.

primary_case.title: Michael I. Posner's endogenous/exogenous spatial cueing ('Posner Cueing Paradigm') experiments
primary_case.place: University of Oregon Cognitive Neuroscience Laboratory, Eugene, Oregon

people.name: Michael I. Posner
people.role: Cognitive neuroscientist who proved attention moves across visual space independently of physical eye movements and mapped the brain's three attention networks

people.name: Charles R. R. Snyder & Raymond M. Klein
people.role: Collaborators on valid/invalid cost-benefit chronometry and 'Inhibition of Return' (Posner & Cohen 1984)

people.name: Maurizio Corbetta & Gordon Shulman
people.role: Neuroimaging pioneers who mapped Posner's dorsal top-down vs ventral stimulus-driven frontoparietal orienting networks

core_facts.fact: In his 1980 Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology classic (7th Bartlett Lecture), Michael Posner asked a deceptively simple question: can you aim your visual attention to the side WITHOUT moving your eyeballs a single millimeter?

Participants locked their gaze on a central '+' fixation cross flanked by empty left and right boxes, monitored by electro-oculography (EOG) electrodes beside the eyes so any trial with a real eye movement (>1 degree) was discarded.

Before a target flash appeared inside the left or right box, a cue predicted its side: either a central arrow ('endogenous' voluntary cue, accurate 80% of the time) or a brief peripheral border flash ('exogenous' automatic cue).
Subjects pressed a single detection key the instant the target appeared — requiring zero eye movement and zero left-vs-right hand choice.

Even with eyeballs frozen dead-center on '+', targets landing in the VALIDLY cued box (80% trials) sped up reaction time to roughly ~220-240 milliseconds, versus ~250-265 ms neutral and ~280-305 ms on INVALIDLY cued 20% trials — a ~50-60 ms 'spotlight' swing.
Covert attention began boosting visual sensitivity at the cued spot within 50 to 150 milliseconds — FASTER than the ~200-250 ms human eyes even need to launch a physical saccade.

Four years later (Posner & Cohen, 1984), Posner discovered a brilliant twist on peripheral flashes: for the first ~100-200 ms a flash pulls attention in, but after ~300 ms the spotlight bounces away and INHIBITS that old spot ('Inhibition of Return') so foraging eyes keep scanning fresh ground.

Lesion and fMRI studies localized Posner's covert spotlight to intraparietal sulcus / superior parietal cortex ('disengage'), midbrain/brainstem superior colliculus ('move'), and thalamic pulvinar ('engage'), while modern 'zoom-lens' refinements showed the beam also widens or narrows on demand.

Across Posner's (1980) covert-orienting cueing blocks with eyes held strictly on central fixation, simple target detection averaged roughly 235 ms after valid spatial cues versus roughly 295 ms after invalid cues.

wow_facts.fact: With electrodes proving their eyeballs never budged a millimeter from a center '+', people detected flashes off to the side 60 milliseconds faster simply because an invisible mental spotlight arrived there first.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Seeing sharply doesn't just follow your eyes — your mind arrives before your eyes ever move.

wow_facts.fact: Your covert attention spotlight shifts to a new corner in ~100 milliseconds — twice as fast as the ~220 milliseconds your eye muscles need to physically turn.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Attention scouts the landing pad ahead of every glance.

wow_facts.fact: Flash a bright distraction on the left and wait just 300 milliseconds, and your brain actually becomes SLOWER at that exact spot ('Inhibition of Return').
wow_facts.why_surprising: Evolution built an anti-staring timer so you scan the whole jungle instead of getting stuck on one rustling leaf.

wow_facts.fact: Patients with right parietal cortex damage can still move their eyes and see an object alone — yet fail to 'disengage' Posner's spotlight from the right side when an invalid target appears on the left.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Posner broke 'paying attention' into three separate neural gears: disengage, move, engage.

misconceptions.myth: Whatever your eyeballs point directly at is automatically what you are paying attention to.
misconceptions.truth: Covert attention and eye gaze dissociate completely — athletes, drivers, and magicians exploit that split every second.

misconceptions.myth: Attention only changes which button your hand prepares to press, not how clearly you see.
misconceptions.truth: Posner used a single-key press and later ERP recordings proved valid cues physically amplify early visual cortex sensory waveforms within 80-100 ms.

misconceptions.myth: Attention is a rigid circular beam of fixed size forever.
misconceptions.truth: Eriksen's 'zoom-lens' and split-attention follow-ups showed the parietal beam dynamically zooms narrow (high resolution) or wide (broad field).

misconceptions.myth: A blinking banner ad keeps pulling your attention back to the same corner indefinitely.
misconceptions.truth: After ~300 ms without goal relevance, Inhibition of Return actively suppresses that flashed location.

everyday_hooks: A basketball point guard staring dead-straight at a defender's chest while covertly aiming Posner's spotlight at a cutting teammate on the wing for a no-look pass.
Keeping your eyes steady on the highway lane ahead while covertly monitoring a merging car in the right lane.
How a sleight-of-hand magician uses a dramatic left-hand gesture (invalid 80% cue) to pull your covert spotlight 60 ms away from the right-hand pocket.
Why flashing webpage sidebar ads go 'invisible' to your brain half a second later via Inhibition of Return.
